name: Saying is believing effect
statement: After tailoring a description of someone to an audience's known attitude, communicators later recall the original information as though it matched what they said.
meaning: The paradigm has two steps and the second one is the claim. A participant reads a passage of evaluatively ambiguous behaviour about a target person, learns in passing that the audience likes or dislikes him, and writes a description the audience will use to identify him. That first step, audience tuning, is a fact about messages and nobody disputes it. The claim is about what happens afterwards, when the participant is asked to recall the original passage and produces something skewed towards the audience's view. Echterhoff, Higgins and Levine's shared-reality account says the skew is not a side effect of having written the words. On that account the communicator adopts the audience's view as a version of reality held in common, and does so only when the audience counts as a source worth sharing reality with. The account therefore predicts its own boundary conditions, and the tests of it manipulate whether the audience can be trusted rather than whether the message was written.

origin.who: E. Tory Higgins and William S. Rholes
origin.note: The paper titled the effect and ran at 14(4), 363-378. Its text is closed at Elsevier and Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all record no repository copy, so nothing about its design or its numbers is reported here from the paper itself. Its abstract at ERIC says it examined "whether modifying a message about a stimulus person to suit the listener has a lasting effect on the communicator's own recall and evaluation of this person".

evidence: Echterhoff, Higgins and Groll ran three experiments at the University of Cologne and set out to break the effect. In the first, 65 students described a target called Michael to an absent audience called Armin, then heard ten minutes later that Armin either had or had not picked Michael out from the description. Recall valence, coded by two blind raters on a scale from -5 to +5, split by audience attitude only after success feedback: 0.84 against -0.63, F(1, 61) = 13.41, p < .01, d = 1.23. After failure feedback the means were 0.16 and 0.00, F(1, 61) < 1, and the interaction was reliable, F(1, 61) = 5.44, p < .05. The second experiment gave 66 students an audience who was either a fellow Cologne student or a trainee at a hairdressing school. Both groups tuned their messages. Only the in-group group showed the recall bias, 0.91 against -0.82, F(1, 62) = 16.78, p < .001, d = 1.21, while the out-group means were 0.75 and 0.29, F(1, 62) = 1.17, ns. Trust was measured by asking whether Armin's judgment of other people can be trusted. It was higher for the in-group audience, F(1, 62) = 3.99, p < .05. With trust in the regression the coefficient for group membership fell from a reliable .26 to .17, p = .16, while trust held at .38, p < .01. The authors call that partial mediation, and their Sobel test of it was marginal, z = 1.70, p < .09. The third experiment crossed both manipulations across 127 students. Only the in-group audience with success feedback gave a reliable recall bias, F(1, 119) = 18.02, d = 1.40. The out-group audience with success feedback reached d = 0.62 at p < .07, and the two failure-feedback cells gave d = 0.08 and d = 0.02. Trust mediated the feedback effect there, Sobel z = 1.99, p < .05. Echterhoff, Higgins, Kopietz and Groll later put the same argument to a motivational test. Their abstract at Europe PMC reports four experiments. The memory bias was larger when tuning served shared reality than when it served politeness towards a stigmatised-group audience, an incentive, entertainment or a blatant demand. That abstract attributes the mediation to epistemic trust rather than to rehearsal, retrieval of the original input, source discrimination or contrast.

replication.headline: Message tuning reproduces every time it is looked for. The memory bias that names the effect is conditional, absent in one online study of 165 people and weaker, on a 2025 meta-analysis, with out-group audiences and identity-threatening topics.
replication.detail: Wagner, Axmacher and Echterhoff ran the paradigm online three times. In their first study, 165 participants tuned their messages, t(163) = 5.46, p < .001, and their recall valence did not differ by audience attitude at all, t(163) = 0.73, p = .47. The second study added manipulations designed to build commonality with the audience and recruited 289 people. Message tuning came out at F(1, 277) = 81.66, partial eta squared .228, and the recall bias at F(1, 277) = 4.38, p = .037, partial eta squared .016. The third study, 347 people, gave tuning F(1, 168) = 48.30, partial eta squared .223, and a recall bias among participants who described the target person of F(1, 168) = 12.27, p < .001, partial eta squared .068. These figures are read off the authors' 2021 preprint. The published version, with Higgins added as an author, is in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General and was read in abstract only. Wagner and Echterhoff report three further studies totalling 1,070 participants. Their abstract states that the audience-congruent memory bias held whether or not communicators had formed their own judgment of the target first. Figueroa-Grenett, Páez, Haye and Mendiburo-Seguel pooled the literature in 2025. Their abstract reports 27 studies from 13 articles published between 1990 and 2021, giving 55 effect sizes for message tuning and 59 for memory bias in Cohen's d. Audience attitude moved message tuning robustly, while the memory bias diminished with an out-group audience or a topic that threatened social identity. Heterogeneity ran from 21.23% to 88.47%, and the abstract reports indications of publication bias. Liang, Lin and Souma changed the topic from a person to a laptop and ran 57 undergraduates at a Japanese university, six of whom were excluded. Message valence and impression valence moved with audience attitude, entitativity and epistemic trust in a three-way interaction. For recall valence the paper reports no significant main effect, two-way interaction or three-way interaction at any step. Ye, Zhao, Huang and Meng used Chinese stereotype material. In their first experiment 40 students were recruited and 39 analysed, and recall of stereotype-related information followed the audience's attitude, F(1, 37) = 14.78, p < .001, while recall of neutral information did not, F(1, 37) = 1.97, p = .17. Figueroa-Grenett, Haye Molina, Páez Rovira and Muller moved the topic to national history. Their abstract reports both tuning and memory bias overall, and neither among participants high in nationalism. Yin and Liu ran the paradigm with 70 students in China and report an audience-attitude effect on recall of F(1, 68) = 526.581, p < .001, eta squared 0.89. Doege, Echterhoff, Wagner and Hansen ran two pre-registered experiments on construal level, one of them in this paradigm. Their abstract reports that the construal-level manipulation did not significantly affect shared reality in either.

study.cite: Wagner, U., Axmacher, N., & Echterhoff, G. (2021). Biased memory retrieval in the service of shared reality with an audience: The role of cognitive accessibility. PsyArXiv preprint.

limits: Higgins and Rholes's paper was not read for this entry, so no original effect size sits beside the replication figure and the structured comparison this site usually prints is missing. Elsevier returned 403 to it, and Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all record it as closed with no repository copy, checked on 21 September 2026. A candidate scan indexed at CiteSeerX could not be opened, because that host reset every connection from this session. Two statements about that paper reach this page only through Echterhoff, Higgins and Groll's description of it. One is that the bias was still present when recall came two weeks later. The other is that it went away when participants did not actually write the message they expected to send. Echterhoff, Higgins, Kopietz and Groll's four experiments were read in abstract only, so none of their numbers are here. The Wagner figures come from the 2021 preprint rather than the published article, and a revision can change numbers. Three of the papers cited here are open access and were still not read. Wagner and Echterhoff's 2025 Memory article and Doege, Echterhoff, Wagner and Hansen's registered report are both under CC BY at Taylor & Francis, which answered every request with a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall. Figueroa-Grenett and colleagues' Memory article is indexed as green open access at CONICET Digital, and that deposit turns out to be request-a-copy rather than a download. The 2025 meta-analysis is closed at Wiley, which returns the same bot challenge, so its pooled effect sizes are not on this page. The three Cologne experiments used German students, mostly women, in cells of about sixteen, and their out-group was hairdressing trainees. Yin and Liu's recall effect is implausibly large next to every other figure on this page, and their text gives a negative-attitude group of 36 where their Table 1 gives 35. The journal issued a correction to it for a missing citation, missing acknowledgements and an appendix passage. That missing citation points to an OSF project by Zhang, Cui, Wagner and Echterhoff on romantic partners, which is unpublished, so no figure from it appears here. No multi-laboratory or adversarial replication was located in a search on 21 September 2026 covering Crossref, DataCite, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, DOAJ, OSF, PsyArXiv, CONICET Digital and web search.
misreadings: The first misreading is that the effect says people come to believe whatever they say. It is narrower. The material is ambiguous, the audience's attitude is known in advance, and the measure is free recall of the original passage rather than a stated opinion. The second is treating message tuning as the finding. Participants tuned to out-group audiences and after failure feedback in every Cologne experiment, and those are exactly the conditions in which their memories did not shift. The third is reading the boundary conditions as failed replications. Trust in the audience is what the shared-reality account says the bias runs on, so an audience nobody trusts producing no bias is the theory working. The fourth follows from the third: because the bias is conditional it is also fragile, and one recent online study of 165 people found none of it while message tuning came through at p < .001. The fifth is the name. "Saying is believing" also labels a family of self-persuasion exercises in the growth-mindset and attitude-change literature, in which people write arguments for a position and are said to shift towards it. That is a different claim with a different evidence base, and it has its own entry here under self-persuasion.

Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 14(4), 363-378. The paper that named the effect. Closed at the publisher and not read for this entry.

Read in full from the copy on E. Tory Higgins's Columbia page. Source for every number in the first two thirds of the evidence section.
